```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
options(width = 70, useFancyQuotes = FALSE)
```

## Session Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

1. Use R's operators, and know that they work on whole vectors
2. Call functions using named and positional arguments
3. Explain what a function is, and write your own with default arguments
4. Make decisions with `if`/`else`, `if_else()`, and `case_when()`
5. Repeat tasks with `for` loops and `purrr::map()`, and know when you do not need a loop
6. Chain functions together with the pipe `|>`, including its placeholder `_`

## Running Example: Scoring a Survey Scale

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
| Item | Wording | |
|------|---------|---|
| `eng1` | I am enthusiastic about my job | |
| `eng2` | I feel proud of the work I do | |
| `eng3` | Time drags when I am at work | **R** |
| `eng4` | I would recommend this company | |
| `eng5` | I often think about leaving | **R** |
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- 5-point scale: 1 = Strongly disagree, 5 = Strongly agree
- **R** = reverse-worded: agreeing means *lower* engagement
- Goal: reverse-code, then average into one **scale score**
:::
::::

## The Survey Data

```{r}
#| label: survey-data
#| warning: false   # hide 'package built under R version x.y.z' warnings
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)   # dplyr (if_else, case_when) and purrr (map)

survey <- data.frame(
  id           = 1:8,
  department   = c("Sales", "HR", "IT", "Sales", "IT", "HR", "Sales", "IT"),
  tenure_years = c(2.5, 8, 1, 12, 4.5, 6, 0.5, 9),
  eng1 = c(4, 5, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1, 4),
  eng2 = c(5, 4, 2, 5, 3, 4, 2, NA),
  eng3 = c(2, 1, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5, 2),
  eng4 = c(4, 5, 1, 4, 4, 5, 2, 3),
  eng5 = c(1, 2, 5, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
)
```

# Operators {#sec-operators}

## Arithmetic and Assignment

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: arithmetic

5 ^ 3        # exponent
17 %/% 5     # integer division
17 %% 5      # remainder (modulo)
(100 + 200) / (10 - 3) * 10
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: assignment

revenue <- 125000
cost    <- 98000
profit  <- revenue - cost
profit
```
:::
::::

- `+ - * /` as usual; standard order of operations, so use parentheses when in doubt
- `<-` stores a value under a name; assigning to an existing name **overwrites** it
- `=` is used for function arguments: `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`

## Operators Work on Whole Vectors {#sec-vectorized}

```{r}
#| label: vectorized

quarterly_revenue <- c(120, 135, 128, 150)
quarterly_cost    <- c(90, 101, 99, 110)

quarterly_revenue - quarterly_cost       # element by element
quarterly_revenue * 1.05                 # one number applied to every element

6 - survey$eng3                          # reverse-coding a 5-point item!
```

- One of the most useful ideas in R, and why you need fewer loops than you might expect

## Comparison and Logical Operators

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
| Operator | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `<` `<=` `>` `>=` | Comparisons |
| `==` `!=` | Equal, not equal |
| `!` | Not |
| `&` / `|` | And / Or |
| `%in%` | In a set? |
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: logical

survey$eng1 >= 4
survey$eng1 >= 4 & survey$eng2 >= 4
survey$department %in% c("Sales", "IT")

sum(survey$eng1 >= 4)    # count: TRUE = 1
mean(survey$eng1 >= 4)   # proportion
```
:::
::::

## `&&` and `||`

- Work on a **single** `TRUE`/`FALSE` only; used inside `if ()` (@sec-if)

```{r}
#| label: double-and

response_rate <- 0.42
n_responses   <- 168
response_rate > 0.3 && n_responses >= 100
```

- Since R 4.3, a vector of more than one value is an **error**:

```{r}
#| label: double-and-error
#| error: true

survey$eng1 >= 4 && survey$eng2 >= 4
```

### Rule of thumb {.example}
`&` and `|` on vectors and data; `&&` and `||` inside `if ()`.

## Naming Objects and Comments

Names: letters, numbers, `_` and `.`; must start with a letter; **case-sensitive**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Do**

- `snake_case`: `annual_revenue`
- Short but meaningful: `eng_survey`, not `data2`
- Verbs for functions (`reverse_code`), nouns for data (`survey`)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Avoid**

- Names R uses: `c`, `T`, `F`, `mean`, `data`
- Spaces (need backticks)
- Starting with a number or `.`
:::
::::

```{r}
#| label: comments

# Comments explain WHY: pilot stores opened mid-year, so they are excluded
stores <- 44 - 3
```

# Using Functions {#sec-using-functions}

## Arguments: Named, Positional, and Defaults

```{r}
#| label: args-round

args(round)                          # shows the arguments and their defaults

round(3.14159)                       # digits uses its default, 0
round(3.14159, 2)                    # by position: x first, then digits
round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)       # by name, any order
```

### A good habit {.example}
Obvious first arguments by position, everything else by name: `mean(survey$eng2, na.rm = TRUE)`, not `mean(survey$eng2, 0, TRUE)`.

## Reading a Help Page to Call a Function

`?mean`, **Usage** section:

```
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
```

- `x` has no default: you must supply it
- `trim = 0`, `na.rm = FALSE`: defaults used when you leave them out
- `...`: other arguments, passed along

```{r}
#| label: help-page-example

mean(survey$eng2)                    # why NA? na.rm defaults to FALSE
mean(survey$eng2, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Writing Functions {#sec-writing-functions}

## What Is a Function? The Espresso Machine

Press the **two-cup button**: the machine grinds the beans, heats the water, extracts at 20 bar, and pours. **Same steps, same way, same quality, every time.**

| Espresso machine | Function in R |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| The two-cup button | The function's **name** |
| Your choices: number of cups, strength | **Arguments** (inputs) |
| The usual strength if you do not choose | **Default** arguments |
| Grind, heat, extract, pour | The **body** (the steps) |
| Two shots of espresso | The **return value** (output) |
| No need to know how the pump works | You can use `mean()` without reading its code |

## The Syntax

```r
function_name <- function(arg1, arg2) {
  # the body: steps that use arg1 and arg2
  output <- ...
  return(output)
}
```

- `function_name <-` stores the function under a name, like any other object
- `function(arg1, arg2)` lists the inputs
- The **body**, between `{ }`, holds the steps
- `return(output)` sends the result back

## Why Write Your Own?

```{r}
#| label: copy-paste
#| eval: false

survey$eng3 <- 6 - survey$eng3
survey$eng5 <- 6 - survey$eng3     # copied the line above... and forgot to change eng3
```

- The bug is easy to miss: `eng5` is overwritten with the reversed `eng3`
- If the scale changes (say, to 7 points), every copy must be found and fixed
- A function is building the button once: the steps live in one place

### Rule of thumb {.example}
Once you have copied the same code **three times**, write a function.

## A First Function

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: anatomy

profit_margin <- function(revenue, cost) {
  margin <- (revenue - cost) / revenue
  return(margin)
}

profit_margin(125000, 98000)
profit_margin(quarterly_revenue, quarterly_cost)
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
| Part | Example |
|------|---------|
| Name | `profit_margin` |
| Arguments | `revenue`, `cost` |
| Body `{ }` | The calculation |
| Return | `return(margin)` |

- `margin` exists only while the function runs
- Without `return()`, R returns the **last line**: common in others' code
:::
::::

## Default Arguments

Like the machine's usual strength: the value used when you do not choose one

```{r}
#| label: reverse-code

reverse_code <- function(x, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5) {
  reversed <- (scale_max + scale_min) - x
  return(reversed)
}

reverse_code(survey$eng3)                  # defaults: a 1-to-5 scale
reverse_code(c(1, 4, 7), scale_max = 7)    # a 7-point scale
```

- `(scale_max + scale_min) - x` is `6 - x` on a 1--5 scale, `8 - x` on a 1--7 scale

## Recode Missing-Value Codes First

"Prefer not to answer" is often coded `99`. A function does exactly what it was built to do:

```{r}
#| label: missing-code-warning

reverse_code(c(1, 3, 99))
```

### Watch out {.alert}
The `-93` would silently pull down any average it goes into. Replace missing-value codes with `NA` **before** reverse-coding or averaging.

# Making Decisions {#sec-decisions}

## `if` and `else`: One Value {#sec-if}

```{r}
#| label: else-if

response_rate <- 0.42

if (response_rate >= 0.5) {
  print("Excellent response rate")
} else if (response_rate >= 0.3) {
  print("Acceptable response rate")
} else {
  print("Low response rate: send a reminder")
}
```

- For decisions about **one thing**: whether to run a step, which file to read, whether to send a reminder

## `if` Needs a Single Value

```{r}
#| label: if-vector-error
#| error: true

if (survey$eng1 >= 4) print("Agrees")
```

- For a decision about **every element** of a vector, use `if_else()`

## `ifelse()` and `if_else()`: Every Element

```{r}
#| label: if-else-vector
#| error: true

ifelse(survey$eng1 >= 4, "Agree", "Not agree")     # base R
if_else(survey$eng1 >= 4, "Agree", "Not agree")    # dplyr

ifelse(survey$eng2 >= 4, "Agree", 0)        # silently mixes text and numbers
if_else(survey$eng2 >= 4, "Agree", 0)       # stops with an error
```

- `if_else()` is stricter, and lets you handle missing values: `missing = "No answer"`

## `case_when()`: More Than Two Outcomes

```{r}
#| label: case-when

case_when(
  survey$tenure_years < 2  ~ "New",
  survey$tenure_years < 7  ~ "Established",
  survey$tenure_years >= 7 ~ "Veteran"
)

case_when(survey$department == "Sales" ~ "Revenue-generating",
          .default = "Support")
```

### Order matters, and so do missing values {.alert}
The first `TRUE` condition wins, so put specific conditions first. `NA` fails every condition and falls to `.default`: add `is.na(x) ~ NA` first to be explicit.

## `switch()`: Choosing by Name

Picks one option based on a **single** text value; handy for function arguments

```{r}
#| label: switch

summarize_item <- function(x, stat = "mean") {
  result <- switch(stat,
                   mean   = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                   median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                   agree  = mean(x >= 4, na.rm = TRUE),   # proportion who agree
                   NA)                                    # anything else
  return(result)
}

summarize_item(survey$eng1)
summarize_item(survey$eng1, stat = "agree")
```

# Loops {#sec-loops}

## `for` Loops

The **loop variable** (`item`) takes the next value each time around

```{r}
#| label: for-reverse

survey_scored <- survey                    # keep the original unchanged
reverse_items <- c("eng3", "eng5")

for (item in reverse_items) {
  survey_scored[[item]] <- reverse_code(survey_scored[[item]])
}

survey_scored[, c("id", "eng3", "eng5")] |> head(3)
```

- `survey_scored[[item]]`: a column named by a variable (`$item` would look for a column called "item")
- Function = the logic; loop = the repetition; `reverse_items` = the decision

## Storing Results from a Loop

```{r}
#| label: for-store

items <- c("eng1", "eng2", "eng3", "eng4", "eng5")

item_means <- numeric(length(items))       # empty container first
names(item_means) <- items

for (i in seq_along(items)) {              # positions 1, 2, ..., 5
  item_means[i] <- mean(survey_scored[[items[i]]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
round(item_means, 2)
```

### `seq_along(x)`, not `1:length(x)` {.example}
If `x` is empty, `1:length(x)` gives `1 0` and the loop runs on elements that do not exist.

## `while` Loops

Repeats **as long as a condition is `TRUE`**: how many years to double at 7%?

```{r}
#| label: while

balance <- 1000
years   <- 0

while (balance < 2000) {
  balance <- balance * 1.07
  years   <- years + 1
}
years
```

- The condition must eventually become `FALSE`; otherwise press `Esc`

## When You Do Not Need a Loop

```{r}
#| label: no-loop

reversed <- numeric(nrow(survey))          # a loop over respondents: unnecessary
for (i in seq_len(nrow(survey))) reversed[i] <- 6 - survey$eng3[i]

identical(reversed, 6 - survey$eng3)       # the vectorized version

survey_scored$engagement <- rowMeans(survey_scored[, items], na.rm = TRUE)
round(survey_scored$engagement, 2)         # the scale score
```

### Rule of thumb {.example}
Loop over **columns, files, or models**. Do not loop over **rows**: there is almost always a vectorized way.

# Applying a Function to Many Things {#sec-map}

## Base R: `lapply()` and `sapply()`

A data frame is a list of columns, so the function runs once per column

```{r}
#| label: apply-family

lapply(survey_scored[items[1:2]], mean, na.rm = TRUE)   # always a list
sapply(survey_scored[items], mean, na.rm = TRUE)        # simplifies when it can
```

- Common in older code and online answers
- `sapply()`'s output type depends on the results, which can surprise you

## `purrr::map()`: The Recommended Way

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
| Function | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| `map()` | A list |
| `map_dbl()` | Numeric |
| `map_chr()` | Character |
| `map_lgl()` | Logical |
| `map_int()` | Integer |
:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
- Consistent: the name says the output type, or it stops with an error
- `\(x)` is short for `function(x)`: a small **anonymous function**
:::
::::

```{r}
#| label: map

map_dbl(survey_scored[items], \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
map_int(survey_scored[items], \(x) sum(is.na(x)))       # missing per item
```

## The Reverse-Coding Loop with `map()`

```{r}
#| label: map-reverse

survey_scored2 <- survey
survey_scored2[reverse_items] <- map(survey[reverse_items], reverse_code)

identical(survey_scored2[reverse_items], survey_scored[reverse_items])
```

### `for` loop or `map()`? {.example}
Both are fine. A `for` loop is easier to debug when starting out; `map()` is shorter once comfortable. Sessions 5 and 6 add `dplyr::across()` for columns of a data frame.

# The Pipe `|>` {#sec-pipe}

## Functions as Mappings

- A function $f: A \to B$ **maps** each input to an output
- $f(x) = 2x$ doubles; $g(x) = x + 1$ adds one

```{r}
#| label: f-and-g

f <- function(x) {
  return(2 * x)
}
g <- function(x) {
  return(x + 1)
}

f(3)
g(3)
```

## Chaining Functions

"Double 3, then add 1": $g(f(3)) = (g \circ f)(3)$

```{r}
#| label: composition

g(f(3))              # nested: read from the inside out
3 |> f() |> g()      # piped: read left to right, in the order steps happen
```

| Nested | Piped |
|--------|-------|
| `f(x)` | `x |> f()` |
| `g(f(x))` | `x |> f() |> g()` |
| `f(x, y)` | `x |> f(y)` |

### Same result; the difference is readability {.example}
Read `|>` as **"and then."** The left side goes into the **first argument** on the right.

## The Pipe in Practice

```{r}
#| label: pipe

round(mean(survey_scored$engagement), 2)             # mean first, then round

survey_scored$engagement |> mean() |> round(2)       # same, in order

survey_scored |>
  subset(department != "HR") |>
  nrow()
```

## The Placeholder `_`

When the piped value is **not** the first argument:

```{r}
#| label: grow

grow <- function(rate, principal, years = 1) {
  return(principal * (1 + rate)^years)
}

1000 |> grow(0.07, principal = _, years = 10)   # = grow(0.07, principal = 1000, years = 10)

survey_scored |>
  lm(engagement ~ tenure_years, data = _) |>     # formula first, data second
  coef()
```

### `x |> f(y, arg = _)` is the same as `f(y, arg = x)` {.alert}
`_` must be used **with the argument name**: `x |> f(y, _)` is a syntax error.

## `|>` and `%>%`

| | `%>%` (magrittr) | `|>` (base R, 4.1+) |
|--------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Needs a package | Yes (loaded with tidyverse) | No |
| Placeholder | `.` | `_` |
| Placeholder without a name | Allowed: `x %>% f(y, .)` | Not allowed: `x |> f(y, arg = _)` |
| Placeholder more than once | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Parentheses | Optional: `x %>% f` | Required: `x |> f()` |

```{r}
#| label: magrittr-compare

1000 %>% grow(0.07, ., years = 10)              # magrittr: unnamed . works
1000 |> grow(0.07, principal = _, years = 10)   # base R: _ must be named
```

- This course uses `|>`; read `%>%` in older code the same way

# Your Turn {#sec-your-turn}

## Exercise

### Tasks {.alert}
7-point job-satisfaction scale; `js2` and `js4` are reverse-worded; "Prefer not to answer" = `99`

1. Write `clean_missing(x, missing_code = 99)` that replaces `missing_code` with `NA`
2. Use a `for` loop to apply `clean_missing()` to all four items
3. Reverse-code `js2` and `js4` with `reverse_code()`. Which argument must change?
4. Use `map_dbl()` to compute each item's mean, ignoring missing values
5. Create `satisfaction`, each respondent's average, with `rowMeans()`
6. `case_when()`: below 3 = `"Low"`, 3 to below 5 = `"Medium"`, 5 or above = `"High"`
7. **Bonus:** run step 3 *before* step 2 on fresh data. What happens to the `99`s?

## Exercise Data

```{r}
#| label: exercise-data

js <- data.frame(
  id  = 1:6,
  js1 = c(6, 2, 7, 99, 5, 3),
  js2 = c(2, 6, 1, 3, 99, 5),
  js3 = c(5, 3, 6, 4, 6, 2),
  js4 = c(3, 7, 2, 4, 2, 99)
)
```

## Exercise: Solution (1--4)

```{r}
#| label: exercise-solution-1

clean_missing <- function(x, missing_code = 99) {            # 1.
  x[x %in% missing_code] <- NA
  return(x)
}

js_items <- c("js1", "js2", "js3", "js4")
for (item in js_items) js[[item]] <- clean_missing(js[[item]])   # 2.

for (item in c("js2", "js4")) {                               # 3. scale_max = 7
  js[[item]] <- reverse_code(js[[item]], scale_max = 7)
}

map_dbl(js[js_items], \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))             # 4.
```

## Exercise: Solution (5--7)

```{r}
#| label: exercise-solution-2

js$satisfaction <- rowMeans(js[js_items], na.rm = TRUE)       # 5.

js$satisfaction_level <- case_when(                          # 6.
  is.na(js$satisfaction) ~ NA,
  js$satisfaction < 3    ~ "Low",
  js$satisfaction < 5    ~ "Medium",
  .default               = "High"
)
js[, c("id", "satisfaction", "satisfaction_level")]
```

**7.** Nothing stops you: each `99` becomes `8 - 99 = -91`, silently dragging those scores far below the 1--7 range. Clean missing-value codes first.

# Summary {#sec-summary}

## Key Takeaways

- **Operators work on whole vectors.** `&` and `|` on vectors; `&&` and `||` only inside `if ()`
- **Obvious arguments by position, the rest by name**; the help page's Usage shows defaults
- **A function is an espresso-machine button**: same steps, every time. Copied code three times? Write one
- **Recode missing-value codes such as `99` to `NA` before computing anything**
- **`if` decides about one value; `if_else()` and `case_when()` about every element**
- **Loop over columns, files, or models, not rows.** `map()` is a shorter alternative
- **`x |> f() |> g()` is `g(f(x))`**, in the order steps happen; `arg = _` pipes into another argument
